analysis.one_liner: Requires federal investigations of major airlines accused of crushing new low-fare competitors at hub airports.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in May 1999 with three cosponsors, it was referred to the House Aviation Subcommittee and died there when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the Secretary of Transportation to open an investigation whenever a big hub airline responded to a new low-fare competitor in ways the bill flagged as predatory — for example, flooding a route with cheap seats until the incumbent's own revenue from the route dropped below what a reasonable response would have produced [S2][S3]. Lawmakers in the 1990s accused major carriers of matching startup airlines' fares, absorbing losses at their hubs, and driving the new carriers out, after which fares went back up [S2]. The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Travelers at hub airports dominated by one or two major carriers, where fares are typically highest, could benefit if mandatory investigations deterred the incumbents from driving out low-fare rivals. New entrant airlines — carriers flying scheduled service for fewer than ten years with a low-fare strategy — would gain an enforcement backstop against being undercut out of a market [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Would require the Transportation Secretary to automatically investigate a major carrier competing with a new entrant at the major carrier's hub if the major carrier added capacity and sold so many seats at very low fares that its own local revenue fell below a reasonable alternative response [S2][S3].

A second trigger applies when the major carrier carried more passengers at the new entrant's low fares than the new entrant's total seat capacity or its own low-fare passenger count, again with lower local revenue than a reasonable response would have produced [S3].

The definitions target exactly the incumbents-versus-startups dynamic: a 'new entrant' is a carrier flying scheduled service for under ten years with a low-fare strategy, and a 'hub airport' is one with at least 0.25% of total annual U.S. boardings [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Major hub carriers would bear the cost of mandatory investigations and possible enforcement whenever their fare-matching fit the bill's triggers. Travelers could also pay indirectly: the trigger is based on revenue lost through matching low fares, so an incumbent facing investigation on every price cut might hold fares higher rather than match a rival — the trade-off an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

drawbacks.text: The bill's trigger is built on the incumbent's own revenue falling after it matches low fares, which could chill legitimate price competition: an airline that simply cuts fares aggressively to win customers fits the pattern the bill targets, so the threat of automatic investigation could deter fare cuts that benefit travelers [S3].

The bill only mandates investigations, not penalties, and includes an exception letting the Secretary skip an investigation when there are strong reasons to believe the carrier's response does not violate the unfair-competition standard — so its practical effect on airline behavior was uncertain even on paper [S3].
Distinguishing predatory pricing from ordinary competition is notoriously difficult, and rules aimed at it can end up protecting high fares rather than competition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real and widely cited problem — dominant hub carriers allegedly using temporarily low fares to eliminate new competition — but its remedy was procedural: mandatory investigations with a revenue-based trigger and a discretionary escape clause. Whether that would have lowered fares or mainly scared airlines into keeping fares high is genuinely unclear, and the bill never got far enough for anyone to find out.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced, sent to the Aviation Subcommittee the next day, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Sweeney introduced the bill on May 4, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
The next day, May 5, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation, where the record shows no further action.
No committee vote, floor vote, or companion Senate action appears in the bill's history, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill still in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major hub airlines, which faced no new requirement to justify fare-matching campaigns against startup competitors, and committee leaders, who avoided a politically sensitive fight over airline pricing.

for.name: Rep. John E. Sweeney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require Transportation Department investigations of major carriers' responses to new low-fare competitors.

for.name: Three House cosponsors (2 Republicans, 1 Democrat)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill was sent to the Aviation Subcommittee and sat there for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny — a Republican sponsor with two Republican and one Democratic cosponsors — so no party ever took a recorded position on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have made fare-matching campaigns against new entrants at their hubs an automatic investigation trigger, raising the risk of enforcement around the pricing behavior that keeps hub fares high. Its death left their pricing discretion untouched.

Carriers under ten years old pursuing low-fare strategies would have gained an enforcement backstop against being undercut out of markets they entered. With the bill dead, they kept bearing the full cost of competing against incumbents' fare matches.

Travelers at concentrated hub airports stand to gain when low-fare competition survives; the bill's enforcement mechanism was designed with their fare levels in mind. The risk on the other side is that predatory-pricing rules can deter legitimate fare cuts.
